title: Which tests earn their place
question: Which kinds of warning sign are carried by organizations in known cases far more often than by City-paid organizations in general, and which are not?
finding: 72 of 5,149 City-paid organizations (1.4%) are in a known case, and 42 of the 444 profiled nonprofits (9.5%). Of 253 kinds of sign, 40 are carried by at least three known-case organizations at twice or more the rate of other organizations, nonprofits included, even with one case taken away, and 21 of those were also datable before at least two cases became public, led by: Monitoring findings left open in three or more years, or published targets missed (15 of 33 carriers); Monitoring findings left unresolved two years running (9 of 14 carriers); A gift, donation or requested payment in the year one of its contracts was approved (24 of 154 carriers); Identical odd amounts paid twice in one year (20 of 151 carriers); One owner, several names, all paid by the City (17 of 355 carriers). 30 kinds with fifteen or more carriers pick out no more than two known cases, led by: Ten or more purchase orders just under the bidding limit (1 of 106); Large payments soon after registering (2 of 94); Tax return discloses business with an officer or director (2 of 43); The same names on the funder's board and the recipient's (1 of 40); and 17 mark size rather than cases, such as The scorecard: the 60 nonprofits paid most, and what anyone else recorded about their results.
how: City-paid organizations are every payee with at least $100,000 from fiscal 2019 to 2026 that is not a public body, a ledger catch-all or a name that reads as a private person’s, plus every profiled nonprofit and every firm a case file names (5,149 in all). For each kind of sign: how many carry it, how many of those are in a proven, charged or official case, and that share divided by the share of all City-paid organizations in such a case (1.4%). Two further ratios repeat the sum among the 444 profiled nonprofits (9.5% in a known case) and among the 181 of them paid $10 million or more (20.4%), because most signs are computed only for nonprofits and many track size. A sign is called informative when at least three known-case organizations carry it, the ratio stays at two or more with one known case removed (among all organizations and, where nonprofits carry it, among nonprofits too), and it is not merely a mark of size (a ratio under 1.25 among the large nonprofits, or carriers that are simply the largest payees). Weights are 1, 2 or 3, for a one-case-removed ratio of at least 2, 4 and 8. “Years of warning” is the middle gap between the sign’s date and the matter becoming public, where it was dated before.
limits: The known cases are few (72), mostly large nonprofits, and were not chosen at random: they are the ones somebody investigated. A sign can separate them simply because investigators and this project both looked hardest at the same organizations. Ratios are shown beside their counts and should be read as rough; a weight is a coarse rank, not a measurement, and one more or one fewer case would move several of them. Signs left out of this table are listed under leftOut with the reason. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
